paras: The dynamiting of the James store at Beggs, Indian Territory, took place on the night of 25 April 1903, when unidentified whites described as whitecaps blew up the new store of a Black family from Alabama. The blast followed nightly posters showing a Black man hanged and also wrecked a neighboring white-owned drug store, though no one was hurt. The family said it would stay, and several Black editors condemned the attack as an assault on Black business.

Beggs was a town of about 800 on the Frisco railroad, twelve miles northwest of Okmulgee; the wire called it "not strictly a white man's town" but noted that no Black people did business there. About three weeks before the bombing a Black family named James arrived from Alabama, described by the wire as a father and three sons and by a Tuscumbia special as Hillard James, his son Jerry and his son-in-law Henry Spriggs. That correspondent wrote that the Alabama legislature had paid the elder James and Spriggs $2,500 for buildings burned in 1902 during the capture of Will Reynolds, who had taken refuge in James's home, and that the family pooled this with Jerry James's savings.

According to the wire, the family built and stocked a store, and a poster then appeared on its door showing a Black man hanging from a telegraph pole, inscribed "You Brought Trouble Here." It reappeared on three successive nights, and the family refused to leave. The Kansas City Journal added that white merchants had tried to buy the Jameses out, then formed a "white-cap society" that posted nightly signs, and that a committee of whites delivered a final warning the day before the blast.
About 9 o'clock on Saturday night a stick of dynamite was set off under one end of the James building, wrecking it and the adjoining drug store of Dr. Post, a white man. No one was injured.

Muskogee officers quietly sent men to Beggs "to quell any possible uprising," and U.S. Marshal Leo Bennett sent deputies to investigate. The wire reported no clue to the bombers, and although the Kansas City Journal predicted arrests, no report of an arrest appears in the coverage. The Jameses stayed in Beggs, and in Tuscumbia their misfortune was said to be "generally regretted, especially by their own color."

White papers took the story from a Muskogee dispatch of 26 April, printed on 27 and 28 April in the St. Louis Republic, the Savannah Morning News, the Birmingham Age-Herald, the Louisville Courier-Journal, the Washington Evening Star and smaller papers. Headlines stressed race trouble and the newcomers: "Band of Whitecaps Use Dynamite" in the Republic, the "Advent of a Colored Merchant" in the Courier-Journal, and residents who "Refuse to Tolerate Negro Storekeeper" in the Denison Review. The Age-Herald called the Alabama family "Game" for refusing to leave, and a Guthrie column reported "a race riot" at Beggs.

Black papers took it up from 1 May as an attack on Black enterprise. The Plaindealer blamed "a few disreputable white ruffians," urged Black men in the Territory to buy repeating Winchesters, and demanded federal damages. The St. Paul Appeal called Beggs a "damnable outrage" of the business color line, while the Broad Ax and Cleveland Gazette blamed jealous whites, the Gazette mocking southern "cbivalry." The Savannah Tribune reprinted the wire as "Dynamite for Negroes," as did the Baltimore Afro-American.
The Western World, a Black weekly in the region, never reported the bombing; on 30 April it praised the James grocery and declared "no race friction" in the Territory.

Accounts differ on the family's capital: $10,000 in the wire, about $20,000 in the Kansas City Journal, and a $5,000 stock in the Plaindealer's editorial. The wire dated the blast Saturday night, 25 April, while the Baltimore Afro-American's later rewrite said Monday night.

reader.title: Dynamiting of the James store at Beggs, Indian Territory
bases: Night-riding whitecaps posted lynching threats on a Black family's store and then wrecked it with dynamite to drive the family from Beggs (A1, A21).

The Muskogee wire (A1, A2) and the Kansas City Journal report built on U.S. Marshal Bennett's information (A21, A28) independently describe the warnings and the dynamiting, and a Tuscumbia special (A13) confirms the family's move to Beggs and the destruction of their store.

accounts.label: Muskogee wire
accounts.gist: A father and three sons from Alabama with $10,000 built a store; after a hanging poster appeared three nights running, dynamite wrecked the store and an adjoining white-owned drug store on the night of 25 April; the family said it would stay.

accounts.label: Kansas City Journal (from U.S. Marshal Bennett)
accounts.gist: J. W. James and three sons brought $20,000 and bought a livery barn and business houses; indignant white merchants tried to buy and bully them out, formed a white-cap society that posted nightly signs, sent a committee with a final warning, and blew up the store a half hour after closing.

accounts.label: Tuscumbia correspondent
accounts.gist: The family were Hillard James, his son Jerry and son-in-law Henry Spriggs, who had moved from Tuscumbia after the Alabama legislature reimbursed them for property burned in 1902 and had opened a store and brickworks.

accounts.label: Black territorial weekly
accounts.gist: The Western World praised the James & Co. grocery and its families from Tuscumbia and reported no race friction in the Territory, without mentioning the dynamiting.

framing.detail: The St. Louis Republic headed its special 'Band of Whitecaps Use Dynamite' with the deck 'Citizens Indignant Because African Came There, Built a Store and Proceeded to Go Into Business.'

Most white papers ran the Muskogee wire under headlines such as 'Store of Negroes Was Wrecked With Dynamite' and 'Race Trouble Is Imminent', the Birmingham Age-Herald adding that the Alabama family were 'Game, However, and Refuse to Leave.'
The Denison Review headed its version 'Beggs Residents Refuse to Tolerate Negro Storekeeper in Their Midst', and a Guthrie brief called it 'a race riot'.
The Montgomery Advertiser's Tuscumbia special described the family as of good reputation and their misfortune as 'generally regretted'.
The Plaindealer blamed 'white ruffians', urged every Black man in the Territory to buy a repeating Winchester and demanded federal reimbursement.
The St. Paul Appeal used Beggs as the 'most notable instance' of the business color line and called it a 'damnable outrage'; the Broad Ax and Cleveland Gazette blamed jealous whites.
The Savannah Tribune and Baltimore Afro-American reprinted the wire, the Tribune under 'Dynamite for Negroes'.

conflicts.note: The Muskogee wire datelined 26 April says 'last night'; the Afro-American's later condensed rewrite gives Monday, likely an editing error, as no other paper does.
